newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian PM's party votes despite looming split.
newsitem.headline: Indian PM's party votes despite looming split.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's party prepared on Thursday to choose a leader in an election overshadowed by corruption allegations and the prospect of a bitter split in its ranks.
Leaders of the Janata Dal, the largest group in Gujral's 15-party United Front coalition, were set to use the ballot box for the first time in the party's nine years to select their leader.
But the dose of democracy, imposed by an activist Election Commission, was obscured by the incumbent party leader's call to boycott the polls.
Janata Dal president Laloo Prasad Yadav, who is chief minister of the populous eastern state of Bihar, said voter lists had been rigged against him.
"I will not allow anybody to capture the party through proxy and that is why I have given the call for boycott of the elections," Yadav said on Wednesday.

Yadav's supporters in Bihar said they would hold their own convention on Saturday in the state capital Patna to re-elect him as leader of their faction. Results of the balloting in the main faction were not expected before Sunday.
Yadav and 55 others have been indicted by federal police in a $280-million corruption case involving the alleged embezzlement of state animal husbandry funds.
Last month, the case forced a junior minister to resign from Gujral's two-month-old government. But Yadav, who says he is innocent, has refused to step down either as chief minister or party leader.
Newspapers underscored the tension that had built between Yadav and the main contender, Sharad Yadav, who is also from Bihar but no relative.

"Mr (Laloo) Yadav decided to complain against the constitution of the electoral college only after his efforts to have himself anointed as party chief failed and, much to his chagrin, he found that Mr Sharad Yadav had thrown his hat into the ring," The Hindu newspaper said in an editorial.
"It is clear that the dispute that is being witnessed in the Janata Dal is merely a feud between two factions."
Gujral has tried to keep above the fray for fear of being dragged into a fight that could jeopardise his tenuous hold on power.

The Asian Age newspaper said "a formal split will make the Gujral establishment weaker, unless of course Mr (Laloo) Yadav, after splitting the party, still decides to lend his faction's support to the United Front".
Political analysts said Laloo Yadav was not expected to withdraw his crucial support to the centre-left alliance.
But continued tension in the coalition's main party would doubtless complicate Gurjal's task and could embolden its make-or-break ally, the Congress party.

Congress chief Sitaram Kesri, who was scheduled to meet state party leaders on Thursday, wanted his party to review its ties to the ruling coalition in light of the upheaval in Gujral's party, newspapers said.
